Taxi Associations vs Motorists

By: Busisiwe Gumede | Commission

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
From violence to intimidation, taxi associations will stop at nothing to maintain their grip on the transportation market. They say carpooling and lift-clubs are affecting their business.

Unique Selling Point:
In a country plagued by traffic congestion and rising fuel costs, carpooling and lift clubs seem like a logical solution. However, taxi associations are waging a fierce battle to prevent motorists and commuters from sharing rides, even going so far as to intimidate and harass those who dare to defy them.



Summary:
Taxi associations, determined to protect their profits, have launched a campaign of intimidation and harassment against motorists who dare to share rides.

Some commuters said they have encountered situations where mini-bus taxi operators have tried to prevent them from carpooling, being in lift clubs and even, in some instances, ordinary motorists giving lifts to friends and colleagues.

The victims are not just carpoolers, but anyone who happens to have more than two people in their vehicle. Pedestrians who accept lifts from acquaintances are also being targeted. The taxi associations' tactics range from verbal threats and physical assaults to vandalism and even violent attacks.

Further information:
We expose of the taxi associations' reign of terror and the ordinary people who are fighting back against their bullying tactics.

Press Release:


Terrorised by Taxis
It’s a never-ending battle: taxi-operators versus motorists. Now in some parts of Gauteng, taxi associations are shifting gear and redirecting their anger at motorists who share rides with their colleagues, friends or family. As they battle to maintain an iron grip on the public transport market, taxi operators say that carpooling and lift-clubs are impacting their bottom line, robbing them of potential clients. And as the threats escalate, all motorists with more than one passenger in their vehicle could become targets.
Producer: Busisiwe Gumede-Chizhanje| Presenter: Macfarlane Moleli

Script:


VO: You could say that Joburg’s streets belong to the taxi drivers.


Breather:


VO: They have a long track record of reckless driving, intimidation and even violence.


Breather, a short upsound or two.


Already infamous for intimidation and reckless driving, they’re targeting motorists they see as a threat to their profits.




BREATHER


VO: A situation in which simple car journeys end in traumatic confrontations.




UPSOUND Sinenhlanhla
18:42
If someone had pulled a gun out, what would have happened to my father.


VO - Sinenhlanhla Mthethwa lives in Daveyton, on Joburg’s east rand, and travels to work in Sandton by taxi. On her way home with a friend a few weeks ago, it started to rain.


– VICTIM
01:51 I'm like, let me call my dad so you can come and pick us up at where the taxi is going to drop us off, which was going to be easier for us to get home.


VO – They waited for Sinenhlanhla's father at a garage close to a taxi rank. Seconds after they got into his car, a man blocked their way.


SINENHLANHLA MTHETHWA – VICTIM
03:19 and he is like, stop, stop,
03:46 Then this guy that was blocking us comes and tries to pull out the key from the car..


VO – A struggle ensued.


00:03:56:01 - 00:04:06:22
My dad grabs his hand. He's like let go of my key. I told you I'm not an Uber. So they wrestle. They wrestle the wrestle. And my dad ends up getting his key back

00:05:02:14 - 00:05:17:07
He apologized like, no, no, we were not trying to attack you and whatnot. Then this guy starts insulting me. [...] 05:17 This little bitch…

Mac: This happened in front of your dad?

Sine: In front of my dad. That's when I lost it.


VO: This wasn’t an attempted hijacking. The man was a taxi driver - and he thought Sinenhlanhla’s father was driving paying passengers.






VO – Father and daughter finally managed to convince the man that the car was a private family vehicle.
Later that day, adrenaline still pumping, Sinenhlanhla took to social media.


SINENHLANHLA MTHETHWA – VICTIM
00:11 – Right now, I'm shaking…





UPSOUND SINENHLANHLA
00:06:32:06
It was like I'm in the scene all over again. And that's when the video came about to say, this is not the first time I it has. I happened before...


I don't know who this is going to reach but I think it’s high time that we stop being bullied by taxi men.


VO Her post reached further than she could have imagined, with more than fourteen thousand comments, many sharing similar experiences…


CACOPHONY OF VOICES:
“...its daily thing in Mamelodi…”
“...I needed to pay or else they take the car…”
“...my sister experienced the same thing…”
“...they forced him to pay R5000…”
“Did they claim you were lifting other people?’’


VO: From social media to the airwaves, it’s a growing trend.


UPSOUND 702
BONGANI: Kevin you are in edenvale..taxi operators? What are they doing?
CALLER: 0;11 My driver phoned me this morning and saying taxi operators…are stopping vehicles and telling passangers to get out.
BONGANI: What?
CALLER: 0:45 It’s just really bizarre.
BONGANI: 01:15 So now your workers are stuck wherever this happened and they can't get to work?
CALLER: That’s right


VO: It comes down to competition.


UPSOUND – taxi driver inside motorist vehicle…part where the driver asks about passengers.


VO As far as taxi drivers are concerned, motorists with passengers are stealing fare-paying commuters and denting their profits.


UPSOUND – taxi driver and motorist altercation – demanding she drives to their office.


VO Friends – colleagues – families sharing a ride – even a truck driver picking up a hitch-hiker… any vehicle carrying passengers is under threat.


LINK ONE - Sharing a ride is certainly not a crime, but taxi associations are treating it like one. From verbal threats to physical intimidation, what’s driving this reign of terror?
BREATHER


MAC - Thokozani, we are parked at a traffic circle. Explain to us what we are doing here?
Thokozani - We are here to inspect the taxis and to make sure that they are adhering to the rules. And that they are not speeding.


VO Minibus taxis and their drivers belong to associations, which manage routes, set fees and supposedly protect commuters.
Not far from Sandton, we filmed officials of the Alexandra, Randburg, Midrand and Sandton taxi association, ARMSTA, enforcing the association’s rules.
Heading up the operation is Thokozani Mkhize. He believes they’re simply protecting their livelihoods.


MAC: Do you also stop motorists in private vehicles who give pedestrians lifts here in Alexandra?
Thokozani - There are some who take chances and transport people in their private vehicles. That is totally wrong.
MAC: Would it be okay if i gave someone I know a lift?
Thokozani: Yes, that’s fine.


VO - This woman - who asked us to hide her identity - learnerd the hard way a few months ago.


UPSOUND VICTIM
They took out guns and the other one who was a pedi speaker was like, 'you'll find out who you are actually dealing with'


VO: A newcomer to the East Rand, she gives occasional lifts to her neighbours, who help pay for petrol in return. One day, they were stopped by armed men.


VICTIM
02:25 - … they said, Do you know we own the roads?
02:46 I said, No, I'm just going to Kempton Park. Then they said,we’re taking the vehicle to to our offices in Benoni, and you will have to pop out like R15,000.


.VO – Her neighbours were chased away and she was left alone.


M: 05:47, when all of this is happening, what are you feeling? What's going on in your mind?
05:47 My mind was blank because I was I was scared, because hearing stories from different people, how these people act? Yeah, I was scared. … they kill people. So I thought maybe I was their victim, the next victim.


VO: The men eventually let her go, but kept her car.


VICTIM
05:16 … I started borrowing another 2000 from people so that I can give them 3000.


VO - She raised R5000 to get her car back - but she’s still paying off the debt.


VICTIM
11:44 ... after that, I heard again different stories “ahh girl, welcome to the hood, there are a lot of victims, you’re not the first one this has happened to”.


VO: The South African National Taxi Council, SANTACO, is the closest thing to a regulatory body for the industry. Rebecca Phala is the spokesperson.




Breather


REBECCA PHALA – SANTACO
01:47 … It adds on to the very concerning narrative that South Africans have about the taxi industry to say our operators are law unto themselves.


REBECCA PHALA – SANTACO
M: 02:13 So then what measures are you guys putting into place to ensure the safety of commuters?
02:20 So the first thing we do is as and when our drivers mainly are found to have essentially violated a fellow South African, the first thing we appreciate and encourage people must open cases with law enforcement, right? Because that is criminality. But secondly, in terms of what the industry does is we've got disciplinary processes that are undertaken internally. We also urge south africans to reach out to local associations to register their concerns.


LINK TWO - Who's in control of your car? You or the taxi associations? They're not just regulating their own industry, they're dictating how normal motorists like you should ride in their own cars. Telling you who you can and can't give a lift to.


VO - Taxi drivers can be suspended or even permanently removed. But according to our sources, investigations aren’t followed through.


UPSOUND ANONYMOUS VICTIM
MAC: Did anyone from SANTACO call you?
VICTIM: No, no one called.


SINENHLANHLA MTHETHWA – VICTIM
09:58 ... I did get a call from the Santaco office. About three or four days later, nothing ever happened.


VO - The association’s disinterest in this case is perhaps unsurprising. While not condoning criminality, it appears to share the controversial views of its drivers.


MAC: Sometimes it’s an act of kindness - it’s raining. It’s my car, I can do whatever I want with it.
REBECCA: R: 37:34 yes, so you're quite right. It is your car. You should be able to do what you can with it. The criminality, we must make it clear, is not supposed to happen. But again, you're not supposed to transport, it's your mandate as a civilian, to transport another civilian.


VO: But there’s no legal basis for this opinion. Although all public transport operatives need a permit to carry passengers, there’s no law against motorists giving a lift to friends or pedestrians.


BREATHER


In fact, according to Gauteng Traffic Police spokesperson, Sello Maremane, it’s the taxi association bullies who are breaking the law.


UPSOUND SELLO
07:31 an ordinary member of the public is not allowed to stop a vehicle.
08:34 And sometimes they even go to an extent of extorting money from the drivers. It's illegal. It's something that we are clamping on.
M: 07:11 Reports of intimidation and threats by these taxi associations. How have you responded to it as a department then?
S: 07:18 Well, what we did, we have arrested quite a number of them, I must tell you, in the previous financial year, when I checked my stats, almost over 50 taxi operators were arrested in the province for stopping vehicles illegally


VO: He says law enforcement can’t fix the problem alone.


UPSOUND SELLO
12:48 We also want to make an appeal to ordinary members of the public. They should not give any taxi operators money.


VO - But motorists simply don’t trust the police.




VICTIM
A:09:07 I didn't try to call for the police, because we know how rotten our law enforcement people are.


VO And suspicions aren’t helped by the fact that taxi association henchmen often wear what appears to be police uniform.


UPSOUND: Road block video


It's a very volatile industry, I must say, even sometimes our law enforcement officials might get to be in trouble. But we are not going to fold our arms and just look at these people and while they do all sort of criminal activities.


VO - But the victims we spoke to say that’s not evident on the ground.


VICTIM
15:34 … I need to get justice, at the end of the day. I don't owe them, at the end of the day, that money belongs to me. One thing that I want to see happening. I want my money back, and I need justice.


VO – Meanwhile, motorists are on their own - and realistically, there's not much they can do to protect themselves.


SINENHLANHLA MTHETHWA – VICTIM


MAC: 24:46 Since taking that video and hearing other people’s stories… How do you still get in a taxi?
SINE 24:50 get into a taxi. I don't have a choice. I do not have a choice. I still need to get to work.


END.

metadata.One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...): From violence to intimidation, taxi associations will stop at nothing to maintain their grip on the transportation market. They say carpooling and lift-clubs are affecting their business.
metadata.Unique Selling Point: In a country plagued by traffic congestion and rising fuel costs, carpooling and lift clubs seem like a logical solution. However, taxi associations are waging a fierce battle to prevent motorists and commuters from sharing rides, even going so far as to intimidate and harass those who dare to defy them.
metadata.Summary: Taxi associations, determined to protect their profits, have launched a campaign of intimidation and harassment against motorists who dare to share rides. Some commuters said they have encountered situations where mini-bus taxi operators have tried to prevent them from carpooling, being in lift clubs and even, in some instances, ordinary motorists giving lifts to friends and colleagues. The victims are not just carpoolers, but anyone who happens to have more than two people in their vehicle. Pedestrians who accept lifts from acquaintances are also being targeted. The taxi associations' tactics range from verbal threats and physical assaults to vandalism and even violent attacks.
metadata.Further information: We expose of the taxi associations' reign of terror and the ordinary people who are fighting back against their bullying tactics.
